title: “Left-Wing” Communism: an Infantile Disorder
author: V.I. Lenin
shortDescription: Written in 1920 for the Second Congress of the Communist International, Lenin's classic treatise critiques sectarian 'left' radicalism and outlines pragmatic, principled revolutionary strategy and tactics.
subject: Party Strategy & Tactics
context: Written in April to May 1920 in preparation for the Second Congress of the Communist International (Comintern), 'Left-Wing' Communism: An Infantile Disorder addressed young communist parties in Western Europe (especially Germany, Britain, Italy, and the Netherlands). Many newly radicalized activists rejected participation in reactionary trade unions and bourgeois parliaments, refusing all political compromises. Drawing on 17 years of Bolshevik history, Lenin demonstrated that uncompromising ultra-leftism isolates revolutionaries from the working class and leads to defeat.
relatesToToday: Applies to modern political tactics: whether to boycott elections, work inside mainstream trade unions, or form coalitions. Lenin warns against purist, all-or-nothing posturing, arguing that effective organizers must meet working people where they are.
keyTakeaways: Bolshevism succeeded through a synthesis of granite Marxist theory and 15 years of diverse, practical mass struggle.
Iron discipline and centralism in a vanguard party require deep connection with the working masses and proven tactical correctness.
Ultra-left sectarianism ('infantile disorder') mistakes one's own advanced consciousness for the consciousness of the working masses.
Revolutionaries must participate in reactionary trade unions and bourgeois parliaments whenever necessary to reach and educate the masses.
Compromises are unavoidable in real politics; the key is distinguishing tactical retreats that preserve strength from opportunist surrenders.
